{{short description|Mnemonic device for calculating 3 by 3 matrix determinants}}
[[File:Sarrus ABC red blue solid dashed.svg|alt=|thumb|''Rule of Sarrus'': The determinant of the three columns on the left is the sum of the products along the down-right diagonals minus the sum of the products along the up-right diagonals.]]
In [[matrix theory]], the '''rule of Sarrus''' is a [[mnemonic device]] for computing the [[determinant]] of a <math> 3 \times 3 </math> [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] named after the French mathematician [[Pierre Frédéric Sarrus]].<ref name="Fischer"/>

Consider a <math> 3 \times 3 </math> matrix
:<math>M=\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{bmatrix} </math>

then its determinant can be computed by the following scheme.

Write out the first two columns of the matrix to the right of the third column, giving five columns in a row. Then add the products of the diagonals going from top to bottom (solid) and subtract the products of the diagonals going from bottom to top (dashed). This yields<ref name="Fischer">{{cite book |last=Fischer |first=Gerd |title=Analytische Geometrie |publisher=[[Springer Vieweg Verlag|Vieweg]] |year=1985 |isbn=3-528-37235-4 |edition=4th |location=[[Wiesbaden]] |page=145 |language=de}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Cohn |first=P. M. |author-link=Paul Cohn |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KSL6tGj1MnAC&pg=PA69 |title=Elements of Linear Algebra |date=1994-07-01 |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |isbn=978-0-412-55280-9 |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>
\begin{align}
\det(M)= \begin{vmatrix}
a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i
\end{vmatrix}=
aei + bfg + cdh - gec - hfa - idb .
\end{align}
</math>

[[File:Sarrus_rule_vertical.svg|thumb|right|Alternative vertical arrangement]]
A similar scheme based on diagonals works for <math> 2 \times 2 </math> matrices:<ref name="Fischer"/>
:<math>\begin{vmatrix}
a&b\\c&d
\end{vmatrix}
=ad - bc </math>

Both are special cases of the [[Leibniz formula for determinants|Leibniz formula]], which however does not yield similar memorization schemes for larger matrices. The determinants of 4x4 matrices can be found by expanding the most convenient row or column by cofactors and then applying the rule to each of the resulting determinants. (especially if there are elements in the matrix that are zero). For matrices beyond 4x4 it becomes impractical except for specific cases where there are many zero elements). Sarrus' rule can also be derived using the [[Laplace expansion]] of a <math> 3 \times 3 </math> matrix.<ref name="Fischer"/>

Another way of thinking of Sarrus' rule is to imagine that the matrix is wrapped around a cylinder, such that the right and left edges are joined.
